lessons.title: The New Labour Codes: The 50% Wage Rule and What It Does to Your Salary Structure

children.text: In late 2025 and through 2026, HR teams at IT services firms, banks, NBFCs and thousands of smaller companies across India sent employees some version of the same email: "In line with the new Labour Codes, your salary structure is being revised. Your CTC remains unchanged."

Most people read "CTC unchanged", saw a slightly lower in-hand figure and moved on. But underneath that email is the biggest change to how Indian salaries are built in decades. It changes your gratuity, can change your PF, and changes what your structure means for tax.

body.text: The 50% rule is not a floor under your basic salary. It is a ceiling on how much of your pay can be kept out of "wages".

children.text: Four codes replace 29 laws

India has consolidated 29 central labour laws into four Labour Codes. Two of them matter for your salary slip: the Code on Wages, 2019, which defines "wages", and the Code on Social Security, 2020, which governs PF and gratuity using that definition.

events.title: Code on Wages, 2019 enacted
events.description: Introduces a single, uniform definition of "wages", including the 50% proviso.

events.title: Remaining three Codes enacted
events.description: Industrial Relations Code, Code on Social Security, and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code.

events.title: All four Codes come into force
events.description: The new wages definition starts governing PF, gratuity and other wage-linked benefits.

events.title: Ministry of Labour publishes additional FAQs
events.description: Clarifies what counts in total remuneration for the 50% test, including employer PF and statutory bonus, and that gratuity is kept out.

events.title: Income-tax Act, 2025 takes effect
events.description: Tax rules on salary are renumbered at the same time that employers are restructuring pay.

events.title: Central Rules notified under all four Codes
events.description: Detailed procedures finalised, including the EPF framework aligned to the new wages definition. State rules continue to follow.

children.text: What "wages" means now
The Code on Wages starts by including everything:
Wages (Labour Codes)
means all remuneration you receive, including basic pay, DA and retaining allowance. Then it carves out a closed list of exclusions. Anything not on that list is wages.

markDefs.definition: All remuneration expressed in money, including basic pay, dearness allowance and retaining allowance, minus a closed list of excluded items. If the excluded items exceed 50% of total remuneration, the excess is added back to wages.

body.title: See the full list of exclusions under Section 2(y) of the Code on Wages

children.text: These items are excluded from wages. Items (a) to (i) are the ones tested against the 50% limit.
(a) Bonus payable under any law that is not part of your terms of employment
(b) Value of house accommodation, light, water, medical attendance or other amenities
(c) Employer contribution to any pension or provident fund, and interest on it
(d) Conveyance allowance or the value of any travel concession
(e) Sums paid to cover special expenses of your job
(f) House Rent Allowance
(g) Remuneration under an award or settlement between parties or a court order
(h) Overtime allowance
(i) Commission
(j) Gratuity payable on termination
(k) Retrenchment compensation, other retirement benefits or ex gratia paid on termination
Notice what is not on that list: special allowance. That single fact changes more salaries than the 50% rule itself.

body.caption: Exclusions here means items (a) to (i). Per the Ministry's FAQs, total remuneration includes employer PF but not gratuity.

body.title: Wages or not?
body.question: Under the Code on Wages, which of these components of a typical private sector salary counts as wages?
body.explanation: HRA, employer PF and conveyance allowance are all on the exclusion list. Special allowance is not, so it is wages. This is why structures with a thin basic and a fat special allowance no longer shrink the base for gratuity.

children.text: Case 1: Rahul, where the 50% rule does not bite
Rahul is a software developer in Chennai. His total monthly remuneration is ₹1,00,000, built the old-fashioned way with a low basic.

cells: Exclusions are only 18.6%, so nothing is added back

children.text: Rahul's exclusions are just ₹18,600, far below the ₹50,000 limit, so the 50% rule never triggers. But his wages are ₹81,400, not his ₹30,000 basic, because special allowance counts. For anything calculated on wages, his base has almost tripled.

body.title: Rahul's gratuity entitlement by completed years of service

body.text: Gratuity is still payable only after 5 years of continuous service for permanent employees. Years 1 to 4 on this chart show the entitlement building up, not money you can collect. At 6 years, Rahul's gratuity is ₹2,81,769 on wages versus ₹1,03,846 on basic.

children.text: Case 2: Tanvi, where the 50% rule does bite
Tanvi is a sales manager at an FMCG distributor in Mumbai. Her package leans heavily on a fixed monthly commission. Her total monthly remuneration is also ₹1,00,000.
50% of total remuneration: ₹50,000
Excess over the limit: ₹60,500 minus ₹50,000 = ₹10,500, which is added back to wages
Wages: basic ₹25,000 + special allowance ₹14,500 + add-back ₹10,500 = ₹50,000

body.label: Tanvi's gratuity after 5 years
body.context: On wages of ₹50,000, compared with ₹72,115 if calculated on her ₹25,000 basic alone. The add-back and the special allowance together double it.

body.title: Run the 50% test yourself
body.prompt: Imran is a production supervisor in Pune with total monthly remuneration of ₹80,000: basic ₹20,000, HRA ₹10,000, conveyance ₹3,000, employer PF ₹2,400, overtime allowance ₹30,000 and special allowance ₹14,600. What are his monthly wages under the Code on Wages?
body.explanation: Exclusions = HRA ₹10,000 + conveyance ₹3,000 + employer PF ₹2,400 + overtime ₹30,000 = ₹45,400. The limit is 50% of ₹80,000 = ₹40,000, so ₹5,400 is added back. Wages = basic ₹20,000 + special allowance ₹14,600 + ₹5,400 = ₹40,000. The Ministry's FAQs specifically confirm that overtime is counted in this test.

body.title: Say it correctly
body.textWithBlank: The 50% test checks whether the ___ exceed half of total remuneration. It does not require basic pay itself to be 50%.
body.explanation: The Code caps excluded items like HRA, conveyance, employer PF, overtime and commission at 50% of total remuneration. Many employers still simply set basic at 50% of CTC because it is the easiest way to stay compliant, which is why "basic must be 50%" became the popular shorthand.

children.text: What happens to your PF

This is where most headlines got it wrong. PF contributions are compulsory only on wages up to ₹15,000 a month, which means ₹1,800 a month each from you and your employer. That ceiling has not changed. The Ministry of Labour has said plainly that the Codes do not reduce take-home pay where PF is deducted on the statutory ceiling.

body.title: Does the wages definition change your PF?

columns.label: PF capped at ₹15,000 wages
points: Contribution stays ₹1,800 a month each side
No change in in-hand from PF
Only gratuity and other wage-linked benefits move

columns.label: PF on full pay (voluntary)
points: The EPF framework now uses the broader wages definition as its base
If your employer contributes above the ceiling, PF can rise with the wage base
Employee PF deduction rises, so in-hand falls
Employer or employee can now independently reduce contributions above the ceiling

body.text: How employers apply the new wage base to voluntary PF above ₹15,000 still varies from company to company. Do not assume. Compare your payslips from before and after your restructuring and ask HR in writing which base your PF uses.

children.text: What it means for your tax
The Labour Codes are not tax laws, but the restructuring they trigger has tax effects.

Lower gross salary, so lower tax
Lower gross salary, so lower tax
Counts towards the ₹1,50,000 limit under Section 123 (old 80C), often already used up
Higher basic changes the HRA calculation
Exemption can rise or fall. Chapter 2 shows how

body.title: Rahul gets the email
body.scenario: Rahul's employer writes: "To align with the Labour Codes, from next month your basic will be 50% of total remuneration (₹50,000), HRA will be 50% of basic (₹25,000), employer PF will be ₹1,800 a month (12% of the ₹15,000 ceiling), and special allowance will be ₹23,200. Total monthly remuneration stays ₹1,00,000." Rahul is in the new regime, has been with the company 4 years and 3 months, and pays ₹28,000 rent.
body.prompt: What changes for Rahul in wages, PF, in-hand, tax and gratuity? Is there anything he should ask HR?
body.modelAnswer: Wages: exclusions are now HRA ₹25,000 + employer PF ₹1,800 = ₹26,800, below 50%, so wages = ₹73,200 (basic ₹50,000 + special ₹23,200). That is lower than his earlier ₹81,400, because more pay has moved into HRA, but still far above the old ₹30,000 basic. PF: if it was previously 12% of ₹30,000 basic (₹3,600 each side) and is now capped at ₹1,800, his employee deduction falls by ₹1,800 a month and the employer's ₹1,800 saving moves into cash components, so in-hand rises, though his EPF corpus grows more slowly. Tax: in the new regime, basic, HRA and special allowance are all fully taxable. His gross salary rises by ₹1,800 a month because less employer PF sits inside the ₹1,00,000, so his tax rises slightly. The higher HRA does nothing for him in the new regime. Gratuity: he is 9 months from 5 years, and gratuity will be calculated on his last drawn wages, now ₹73,200. He should ask HR in writing (1) whether his PF is being cut from full basic to the ₹15,000 ceiling and whether he can opt to keep the higher contribution, (2) confirmation of the wage figure used for gratuity, and (3) whether reducing HRA and raising special allowance instead would give him a higher gratuity base, since HRA is excluded from wages.

children.text: Lock it in

cards.definition: All remuneration minus a closed list of exclusions, plus any excess of exclusions over 50% of total remuneration.
If items (a) to (i) of the exclusions exceed 50% of total remuneration, the excess is added back to wages.
Not on the exclusion list, so it counts as wages.
₹15,000 a month. Contributions above it are voluntary. The ceiling is unchanged by the Codes.
Last drawn wages under the new definition, not just basic plus DA.
Payable after 1 year of service under the Code on Social Security, 2020.

body.title: After your restructuring email
steps: Put your old and new salary structures side by side, component by component
List every excluded item (HRA, conveyance, employer PF, overtime, commission) and check whether they exceed 50%
Calculate your wages under the Code, including special allowance
Check which base your PF now uses and whether it is capped at ₹15,000
Confirm with HR the wage figure that will be used for your gratuity
Recalculate your monthly in-hand and adjust SIPs and EMIs if needed
If you are in the old regime, redo your HRA exemption with the new basic

body.text: The Labour Codes and their rules are new, and employer practices, state rules and official clarifications are still evolving. Examples here are simplified illustrations based on the Codes, the Central Rules of May 2026 and the Ministry's FAQs. This lesson is for education and is not legal or tax advice.

points: Four Labour Codes came into force on 21 November 2025, with Central Rules notified on 8 May 2026.
Wages means all remuneration minus a closed list of exclusions. Special allowance is not excluded, so it is wages.
The 50% rule caps exclusions like HRA, conveyance, employer PF, overtime and commission at half of total remuneration. Any excess is added back to wages.
Gratuity is now calculated on wages, which can double or triple it for people with a low basic.
Compulsory PF is still based on the ₹15,000 wage ceiling. Only voluntary contributions above it can rise with the new wage base.
In the new regime, restructuring mostly changes tax through how much employer PF sits inside CTC. In the old regime, HRA and Section 123 (old 80C) effects matter too.
